alternative: Rely on the GC for memory and release external resources deterministically: try-with-resources on AutoCloseable, java.lang.ref.Cleaner (PhantomReference plus ReferenceQueue) for resources a library owns, and JNI global/local references at the native boundary instead of a hand-written count.
idiom_name: none - GC owns lifetime; Cleaner/try-with-resources at the resource edge
implementation_notes: The JVM tracks objects by reachability, not by count: references are traced and no user field can force reclamation, so a hand-written AtomicInteger encodes protocol state at best. What replaces the classic structure: try-with-resources, which calls AutoCloseable.close on every exit path, and java.lang.ref.Cleaner, which registers a cleaning action to run after the object becomes phantom reachable and is the documented modern replacement for finalize; at the JNI boundary the VM keeps its own counted handle tables (local and global references), which is where a native-facing count belongs.
pitfalls: A Cleaner action that captures the instance (anonymous class over fields, lambda closing over this) keeps the object strongly reachable from its own cleaner, so the action never runs; the JDK examples use a static state class for that reason.
Finalization is deprecated for removal and cannot enforce release order: a resource released in a finalizer may outlive everything it was meant to protect.
Try-with-resources is per-scope: an object stored in a long-lived field is never closed by it, and close() must be idempotent because callers may close early.
